title: Timothy's Good News and Paul's Prayer
summary: Unable to bear the uncertainty any longer, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy back to Thessalonica to strengthen the believers and find out whether their faith had survived persecution. Timothy has now returned with good news of their faith and love and their longing to see Paul. Overjoyed, Paul thanks God, prays night and day to see them again, and asks the Lord to make their love overflow and to establish them in holiness until Jesus comes.
story: Chapter 2 ended with Paul torn away from the Thessalonians and hindered by Satan from returning. Chapter 3 tells what he did instead. The chapter completes the long, personal first half of the letter, which began with thanks in 1:2 and ends here with a prayer. It lets us see the anxiety behind Paul's mission: new churches, planted in weeks, left behind under pressure, with no way to know how they were faring. It also explains why this letter was written at all. Timothy's report is the occasion; the letter is Paul's response. The prayer at the end (verses 11 to 13) introduces the two subjects of chapters 4 and 5: love and holiness, and the coming of the Lord.
historical:
After leaving Thessalonica, Paul went to Berea, and when opponents followed him there he was taken to Athens, leaving Silas and Timothy behind with instructions to join him as soon as possible (Acts 17:10-15). Acts next reports that Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia to Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5). This chapter fills in a detail Acts does not mention: at some point Timothy was with Paul in Athens and was sent back to Thessalonica from there. The simplest reconstruction is that Timothy reached Paul in Athens, was sent back to Macedonia, and later rejoined him in Corinth, where Paul wrote this letter around AD 50 or 51.

The persecution the Thessalonians faced (verses 3 and 4) came from their neighbors, as 2:14 says. It was probably not an official, empire-wide persecution, which did not begin until later, but social pressure, hostility, and at times violence from family, trade associations, and fellow citizens who saw the new faith as a threat to the gods and to civic order.
cultural:
Travel in the ancient world was slow, costly, and sometimes dangerous, and there was no public postal system for private letters. Paul could not simply send a message and wait for a reply; he had to send a trusted person, which meant giving up that person's help. His willingness to be left alone in Athens, a city he found full of idols (Acts 17:16), shows how much the Thessalonians meant to him.

Timothy had a particular role as Paul's delegate. He came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1), and was trusted to represent Paul, teach, and bring back reliable news (compare 1 Corinthians 4:17; Philippians 2:19-22). The word Paul uses for Timothy's report in verse 6 is euangelizomai, the verb usually used for proclaiming the gospel. It is the only place in Paul's letters where he uses it for something other than the gospel of Christ, which shows how much this news meant to him.
literary: The chapter has two parts: narrative and prayer. Verses 1 to 5 tell what happened, with the repeated phrase could bear it no longer (verses 1 and 5) framing the section and revealing Paul's anxiety. Verses 6 to 10 describe Timothy's return and Paul's joy, piling up words of relief: good news, comfort, living, thanksgiving, joy. The emotional climax is verse 8: now we can go on living, as if Paul's own life depended on their steadfastness. Verses 11 to 13 are a prayer written in the form of a wish, sometimes called a wish-prayer, addressed to God the Father and the Lord Jesus together. It gathers the chapter's themes (seeing them again, love, holiness) and points toward the coming of the Lord, marking the end of the letter's first half.

outline.t: Timothy sent to strengthen the church
Timothy's good news and Paul's joy
A prayer for reunion, love, and holiness

doctrines.note: Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he warned them persecution would come, and that believers are destined for it (verses 3 and 4). Suffering does not mean God has abandoned them. It was expected, and it tests and strengthens faith.

Paul prays night and day most earnestly (verse 10), and his prayer asks for concrete things: a way back to them, growing love, and hearts established in holiness. Prayer and action go together; he both prays and sends Timothy.

Paul prays that the Lord will establish their hearts blameless in holiness before God at the coming of Jesus (verse 13). Holiness is the goal toward which the Christian life moves, and it is the Lord's work in them, which is why Paul prays for it.

words.note: Sterizo, to establish, strengthen, or make firm. Timothy was sent to strengthen the Thessalonians in their faith (verse 2), and Paul prays that the Lord will establish their hearts (verse 13). The word frames the chapter: what Timothy began through encouragement, God will complete.

Peirazo, to test or tempt. The same verb can mean testing that proves something genuine or tempting that tries to lead someone astray. Paul calls Satan the tempter (verse 5) and fears that under pressure the Thessalonians might have been lured away from faith, making his labor empty.

Parousia, coming or arrival. Paul prays that the church will be blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints (verse 13). The word, used of a ruler's official visit, gives the Lord's return the sense of a royal arrival, and it shapes Paul's hopes for the church.

christ: Paul's prayer in verses 11 to 13 addresses our God and Father and our Lord Jesus together, asking both to direct his way to the Thessalonians. Remarkably, the Greek verb is singular, as though the Father and the Son act as one. Paul then asks the Lord, most likely Jesus, to make their love increase and overflow. Within twenty years of the resurrection, Jesus is prayed to alongside the Father. The chapter ends with the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints, a phrase echoing Zechariah 14:5, where the Lord God comes with all his holy ones. What Zechariah said of God, Paul says of Jesus. Interpreters differ on whether the holy ones here are angels, believers, or both.
questions: Paul says he could go on living now that he knew they were standing firm. Who are the people whose faith matters that much to you?
Paul warned the new believers ahead of time that suffering would come. How might that kind of honesty help people today who are new to faith?
Paul both prayed for the Thessalonians and sent Timothy to them. Is there someone you have been praying for whom you could also go to or help?
